 Mark Cuban's $6M sale taught him one rule about time
 Cuban says ditching his watch after his 1990 software sale was about owning his time, a mindset that persists
 By   Pareesa Afreen 
 Published October 28, 2026 
 Mark Cuban's $6M sale taught him one rule about time The day Mark Cuban sold his first company, he took off his watch and decided never to wear one again. A watch, he reasoned, meant he was working on somebody else's time.
 Cuban told The Diary of a CEO podcast, hosted by Steven Bartlett, that the habit began with the 1990 sale of software company MicroSolutions. Fortune says the deal made him about $2 million, and it launched his career.
 Why Mark Cuban took off his watch?
 Getting rich was never really the goal, he said. He hated being broke and wanted to "control my own time". His parents never had that option. They always owed someone and had to show up at work.
 He wears an Apple Watch now, for the data. But the rule still shapes how he works. He doesn't wear ties. His version of "swag" is being able to tell other people how they dress.
 He prefers emailing over phone calls because it allows him enough time to compose a reply. In an interview in 2016, Cuban stated that his best hack in life is to avoid meetings and calls unless somebody is offering him money.
 Born into a poor family in Pittsburgh, he told Bartlett that he was the "fat kid" who would do whatever to get some recognition. He once wore an obscene T-shirt to his class and even once mended torn jeans using staples.
 Most people continued to ignore him, to the point where someone even identified the wrong picture in his yearbook at school. This motivated him to prove everyone wrong. At Indiana University, he managed to pay for his junior year using a chain letter scheme from his dorm.
 How did the $5.7 billion exit change things?
 After MicroSolutions, he didn't reinvest. He bought a lifetime American Airlines pass and travelled.
 His selling of Broadcast.com to Yahoo in 1999 for $5.7 billion's worth of stock turned him into a billionaire. This also left him free to do whatever he wants. In 2000, he purchased the Dallas Mavericks for $285 million and has since sold a controlling interest in 2023. Currently, he is concentrating his efforts on Mark Cuban Cost Plus Drugs, which sells prescriptions without any pharmacy benefit manager.
 There are limitations to money, he claims. If you are desperately poor, chances are you will be desperately rich. However, he certainly enjoys being rich a lot more than being broke.
